cards.explanation: The answer is that he has magnified himself against the LORD. The LORD says, “Make him drunk, because he has magnified himself against the LORD…” (Jeremiah 48:26). To magnify yourself is to make yourself big, and here it's aimed straight at the LORD. Moab is the one doing it.

The answer is laughingstock. The verse says Moab “…will also become a laughingstock.” A laughingstock is the one everybody points at and chuckles about, and it's not a spot anyone wants. I've been the joke in my own bakery plenty of times, friends, but at least I volunteered.

The answer is shake. The LORD says, “For whenever you speak of him you shake your head.” (Jeremiah 48:27). He's talking about how Moab treated Israel, who was Moab's object of ridicule. A head shake is the little move that says plenty without a word. My mustache can do it too, but it takes longer.

The answer is a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave. The verse says, “Be like a dove that nests at the mouth of a cave.” (Jeremiah 48:28). The people of Moab are told to leave the towns and settle among the rocks. A dove is the bird in this picture, and Minty, one of my cookie cutter kids, is shaped like a dove, so I notice every time.

The answer is False. The LORD says Moab's boasting has nothing behind it: “His boasting is as empty as his deeds.” (Jeremiah 48:30). Verse 29 piles up the words for Moab's pride, and verse 30 says it's futile. It's like a cookie box with a beautiful lid and nothing inside.

The answer is that the LORD will wail and cry out for Moab. That's the surprise in this passage. He says, “Therefore I will wail for Moab; I will cry out for all of Moab…” (Jeremiah 48:31). It comes right after the long list of Moab's pride. I think that's a tender thing to find in a hard passage.

The answer is joy. Verse 33 says, “Joy and gladness are removed from the orchard and from the fields of Moab.” The harvest is the happy time, and the LORD says He has stopped the flow of wine from the presses. I think the loss is felt right in that quiet.

The answer is False. The winepresses of Moab are not ringing with joy. The LORD says, “I have stopped the flow of wine from the presses; no one treads them with shouts of joy…” (Jeremiah 48:33). The joy is gone from the shouting, and the verse even says, “their shouts are not for joy.”

The answer is the waters of Nimrim. Verse 34 says, “for even the waters of Nimrim have dried up.” It's in the middle of the list of places crying out, from Heshbon to Elealeh and on to Jahaz. Dried up water is a quiet kind of bad news.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “…I will bring an end to those who make offerings on the high places and burn incense to their gods.” (Jeremiah 48:35). The incense goes to their gods, not to the LORD. The LORD is the one saying it will end.

The answer is that the wealth they acquired has perished. Verse 36 says the LORD's heart laments for the men of Kir-heres, “…because the wealth they acquired has perished.” The verse says His heart laments like a flute. I think that's a tender way to say it.

The answer is sackcloth. Verse 37 says, “…every head is shaved and every beard is clipped; on every hand is a gash, and around every waist is sackcloth.” Verse 38 adds that everyone is mourning. Sackcloth is rough, scratchy cloth, the opposite of a cozy apron.

The answer is an unwanted jar. The LORD says, “…I have shattered Moab like an unwanted jar…” (Jeremiah 48:38). Everyone on the rooftops and in the squares is mourning. I think this is a heavy picture, so I'll just let it sit.

The answer is an object of ridicule and horror. Verse 39 says, “Moab has become an object of ridicule and horror to all those around him.” Remember verse 27, where Israel was Moab's “object of ridicule”? That phrase shows up again here. It's a serious thing to notice.

The answer is the eagle. The LORD says, “Behold, an eagle swoops down and spreads his wings against Moab.” (Jeremiah 48:40). An eagle is big, fast and hard to outrun. That picture of wings spread wide is a lot to take in.

The answer is the heart of a woman in labor. The LORD says, “In that day the heart of Moab’s warriors will be like the heart of a woman in labor.” (Jeremiah 48:41). These are fighting men, the ones you'd expect to be steady. I think the picture shows how shaken they are.

The answer is False. Verse 44 says, “…whoever climbs from the pit will be caught in the snare.” The verse goes from panic, to the pit, to the snare. It's like getting out of one jam just to land in the next, friends. No easy exits in this verse.
The answer is exile. Verse 46 says, “…your sons have been taken into exile and your daughters have gone into captivity.” Exile means being taken away from home.

The answer is False. The LORD says, “Yet in the latter days I will restore Moab from captivity…” (Jeremiah 48:47). After all that pride and judgment, the passage ends on restoring. The very next line says, “Here ends the judgment on Moab.”
